query: Summarize this paragraph:The ecological diversity of the KSA allows multiple opportunities for the evolution of variation in both mosquitoes and their pathogens. Large-scale movements of people, including the annual pilgrimage to Mecca, large-scale use of foreign workers and new developmental projects engender environmental heterogeneity and complex epidemiology. The wide variation in ecological settings may complicate the understanding of spatial/temporal characteristics and population dynamics of mosquito vectors of pathogens that cause diseases in humans. Investigators may be reluctant to conduct ecological studies in the KSA because field work is labour-intensive and time-consuming. Moreover, due to habitat heterogeneity, which in the KSA is often extreme, there are species of only seven mosquito genera in the country. Here we present the first complete list (see above) of the mosquito species that definitely are known to occur in the KSA. In some cases, ecological and morphological studies have shown that some species are members of species complexes. There are members of four Anopheles species complexes in the country, including the An. gambiae, An. fluviatilis, An. culicifacies and An. subpictus complexes. The Afrotropical An. gambiae complex consists of eight species, which includes malaria vectors (An. gambiae, An. arabiensis, An. bwambae, An. coluzzii, An. merus and An. melas) and non-vectors (An. quadriannulatus and An. amharicus) [70, 71]. Anopheles arabiensis is the only member of the complex with a range that extends outside of Africa into the southwestern and western areas of the Arabian Peninsula, occurring in the KSA and Yemen, where it is the major malaria vector [2, 3, 7, 72,73,74,75]. Most ecological studies conducted in the KSA recorded the presence of An. arabiensis (often as An. gambiae) in different life stages [27, 29, 30, 51]. Moreover, molecular analysis based on the internal transcribed spacer (ITS2) region of rDNA has shown that An. arabiensis (GenBank: KM068071) is the only member of An. gambiae complex present in the KSA [59]. The An. fluviatilis complex is a group of mosquitoes that is widely distributed in southern and southwestern Asia and includes important malaria vectors [76]. The complex includes four species informally denoted as species S, T, U and V [77,78,79,80,81]. Anopheles fluviatilis S is mainly anthropophilic, endophilic and a very competent malaria vector [52]. Species T and U are primarily zoophilic, exophagic and exophilic, and are regarded as poor- or non-vectors of malaria even though they are responsible for malaria transmission in mountainous and hilly areas in Asia, including Iran [80, 82]. Anopheles fluviatilis (s.l.) was recorded in the eastern and western regions of the KSA by Mattingly & Knight [2], Wills et al. [31] and Al-Ghamdi et al. [51]. It is not known whether species T or U or both are present in the KSA. The An. culicifacies complex consists of five sibling species, informally named species A, B, C, D and E, based on cytotaxonomic and molecular evidence [53, 76, 83]. These species have distinct geographical distributions, blood-feeding behaviour and vectorial capacity for malaria transmission [54, 84, 85]. The complex is widely distributed from southern China to Iran, the Arabian Peninsula and Ethiopia [86]. Species E is the most important malaria vector in the Indian subcontinent, and is highly anthropophilic and endophilic [87]. The other sibling species have low anthropophilic index or are highly zoophilic, and are considered poor- or non-malaria vectors in India and Sri Lanka [52, 88]. Available data indicate there are at least two species of the complex in Iran [89], but only the presence of species A has been confirmed based on cytogenetic and molecular evidence; the second species may be a new member of the complex [90]. Further study is needed to determine which member or members of the complex are present in the KSA. The An. subpictus complex consists of four species in India, informally denoted as species A, B, C and D, based on morphological, chromosomal and molecular differences [91, 92]. As is the case in Iran [90], it is not known which species of the complex is present in the KSA. Anopheles stephensi is the main malaria vector in the eastern region of the KSA, but members of the An. fluviatilis and An. culicifacies complexes, which are important malaria vectors in other parts of Asia [2, 3, 55, 74], may contribute to malaria transmission. In Asia, An. stephensi, An. culicifacies (s.l.) and An. fluviatilis (s.l.) consist of different ecoforms that are restricted to rural or urban areas with different degrees of involvement in malaria transmission [54, 76, 85]. Anopheles stephensi is a major vector in Asia and the Middle East, including, in addition to the eastern KSA, areas of Iran, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India and southern China [87]. It includes three ecological variants (egg phenotypes): the mysorensis, typical and intermediate forms, which are based and distinguished on egg morphology [87, 93,94,95,96]. The typical (type) form is mainly found in urban areas, whereas the intermediate and mysorensis forms are mainly found in rural environments [87]. The blood-feeding behaviour and role of these forms in malaria transmission varies in different geographical regions. In Iran, the type form is highly anthropophilic and a major malaria vector, whereas the mysorensis form is mainly zoophilic and a poor- or non-vector [97]. In contrast, the mysorensis form is an important malaria vector in India [98]. These differences might be due to the type of host available and the presence of certain mosquito genotypes with different host preference and susceptibility to malarial parasites. Molecular study using two different markers (ITS2 and cox1) did not reveal any differences between An. stephensi (ITS2, GenBank: KM052589; and cox1, GenBank: KJ528887–KJ528894) in two distant cities of the KSA (Al-Ahsaa and Dammam) where different phenotypes might be present [59]. Anopheles azaniae was first encountered in Saudi Arabia during the collection of mosquitoes for Rift Valley virus isolation in the Jizan Region [17], and subsequently collected in the same region by Alahmed et al. [18] and Khater et al. [7]. The record of this species in the Riyadh Region [32], which is a very large eastern region that shares its southern border with Yemen, requires confirmation. The record of this species in the more northerly western Al-Madinah Al-Munawarah Region [33] is doubtful and a probable misidentification of either An. dthali or An. rhodesiensis rupicolus. Anopheles azaniae was previously known to occur in neighbouring Yemen [14], where two morphological forms were recently discovered, the typical form and a previously unrecognized form not immediately identifiable as An. azaniae [99]. A single specimen of the atypical form had a mixed human/bovine blood meal, indicating that females are anthropophilic and should be considered a potential vector of malarial protozoa. It seems possible that further studies in the southwest of the KSA may detect the presence of the atypical form. A species of the genus Coquillettidia collected in the Eastern Province of the KSA was identified as a species of Mansonia in the study of Wills et al. [31]. According to the online catalogue of the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit [24], only two species of the tribe Mansoniini are known to occur in more or less arid countries of the Middle East, Cq. (Coquillettidia) buxtoni in Israel and Syria and Cq. (Coq.) richiardii in Iran, Syria and Turkey. With that in mind, it seems likely that the generic identification of Wills et al. [31] was based on keys available at the time, e.g. Mattingly [100], which treated Coquillettidia as a subgenus of Mansonia. In view of the proximity of eastern areas of the KSA to Iran, we are confident that the mosquitoes identified as a species of Mansonia by Wills et al. [31] were most likely specimens of Cq. richiardii. Many of the occurrence records for Cx. pipiens and Cx. quinquefasciatus in the KSA are problematic. Culex pipiens generally occurs north of a line transecting the KSA between Jeddah in the west and Al-Hasa in the east. Culex quinquefasciatus occurs in the more southerly region of the Arabian Peninsula, with isolated populations of Cx. pipiens occurring in the southwestern mountains [5]. Introgression occurs between the two species where their distributions overlap in central KSA (see figure 3 in Harbach [101]). Both species exhibit considerable variation in the larval and adult stages, and they cannot always be distinguished with certainty. They are only reliably distinguished by characters of the male genitalia; however, their separation is complicated by the occurrence of hybrid forms in the central transitional zone and eastern coastal region of the country. Hybrids are morphologically more variable than the parental species, and are only reliably distinguished from the parental species by the DV/D ratio calculated from measurements based on the form and relationships of the dorsal and ventral arms of the male genitalia [102, 103]. It is not possible to distinguish hybrid larvae and females from the parental species. For this reason, some hybrid specimens collected in and around the zone of introgression have undoubtedly been misidentified as either Cx. pipiens or Cx. quinquefasciatus. Larvae and adults collected north of the hybrid zone that have been identified as Cx. quinquefasciatus are misidentified specimens of Cx. pipiens, and those collected south of the zone that have been identified as Cx. pipiens, with the possible exception of those collected in the southwestern mountains, are misidentified specimens of Cx. quinquefasciatus. Future studies based on dissections of male genitalia or DNA sequence analysis of larvae and adults are needed to substantiate species identifications and collection records. Culex quinquefasciatus is an important vector of the microfilariae that cause lymphatic filariasis. Culex torrentium is listed as a species of the KSA in the online catalogue of the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit [24] based on a number of reports, including Alahmed et al. [18, 19], Al Ahmed et al. [20, 28], Kheir et al. [34], Alahmed [35] and Hassan et al. [41]. However, it is obvious that the identification of Cx. torrentium in the KSA by these authors is based on unreliable characters of larvae and adult habitus principally using the keys of Harbach [4, 5]. This species can only be distinguished from members of the Cx. pipiens complex with certainty based on features of the male genitalia. Additionally, Cx. torrentium is a Palaearctic species whose distribution only extends south into Turkey and possibly into northern Iran [90, 104, 105]. As noted by Harbach [5], early records of Cx. torrentium in Iraq are doubtful, and the species is not now listed as present in that country [106, 107]. For these reasons, Cx. torrentium is excluded from the list of mosquito species known to occur in the KSA. Four species of the subgenus Culex of the genus Culex occur in the southwestern Afrotropical Region of the Arabian Peninsula, i.e. Cx. decens, Cx. duttoni, Cx. simpsoni and Cx. univittatus. These species were only known to occur in Yemen [5, 108] until they were more recently found in the Asir Region [63], Jizan (Jazan) Region [18] and Najran Province [28], which border Yemen in the southwest corner of the KSA. The records of two of these species, Cx. simpsoni and Cx. univittatus, require confirmation because their identification was based on larvae and adults. They are only reliably distinguished from Cx. sinaiticus and Cx. perexiguus, respectively, based on the morphology of the male genitalia. Records of the two species in more northerly areas of the country are more doubtful. Since Culex salisburiensis has been known to be present in Yemen since 1953 [108], there is no reason to doubt its occurrence in the adjacent Afrotropical area of the KSA [21, 67]. On the contrary, the reported finding of Cx. wigglesworthi in the Asir Region by Al Ashry et al. [67] is certainly a misidentification. The authors collected 4307 Culex larvae, two of which were identified as Cx. nebulosus, three as Cx. perexiguus and two as Cx. wigglesworthi. Larvae were identified using the keys of Hopkins [109], Mattingly & Knight [2] and Harbach [4, 5]. The identification of Cx. nebulosus and Cx. perexiguus may be correct as these two species are included in the keys of Mattingly & Knight (Cx. nebulosus) and Harbach (Cx. nebulosus and Cx. perexiguus). Use of the badly outdated keys of Hopkins [109] for African species published in 1952, leading to the identification of Cx. wigglesworthi, is problematic, nonetheless because it is a sub-Sharan species with closest records in southern Sudan, South Sudan and Kenya. Consequently, as it seems likely that the two larvae were misidentified specimens of either Cx. perexiguus or Cx. univittatus, Cx. wigglesworthi is excluded from the list of mosquito species known to occur in the KSA. Alahmed [35], Alahmed et al. [36] and Khater et al. [7] recorded the presence of Uranotaenia (Pseudoficalbia) unguiculata in eastern and southwestern areas of the KSA. The authors, however, were apparently unaware of the earlier description of Ur. unguiculata pefflyi by Stone [69], and the recognized presence of only that form in eastern parts of the KSA [31]. Consequently, as it is unlikely that the typical form, Ur. unguiculata unguiculata, is present in the country, only the subspecies described and named by Stone [69] is included in the list.

Here's a summary of the Angry Nerds roundup of April 2023 tech stories, organized by week. I've also flagged a few claims in the original that look wrong or questionable.

## April 24
- **SuperNode and CERN:** The Irish superconducting-cable company is working with CERN, through its CIPEA program, on new insulation for superconducting cables. CERN contributes cryogenics and vacuum expertise. The goal is more efficient renewable energy transmission.
- **Software-defined cars:** Software now matters as much as hardware to car buyers. Only about 8% are "petrolheads." Nio's Berlin "house" is a dealership-lifestyle hybrid with coffee bars, meeting rooms, and a kids' play area.
- **AI in healthcare:** Hospitals are using AI for diagnosis and treatment planning. The concerns are biased or limited training data and "AI paternalism," where clinicians defer to AI over patients' lived experience and their own judgment.

## April 17
- **EPA vehicle rules:** The proposed rules aim to close a 1970s fuel-efficiency loophole that favored SUVs and light trucks, and to encourage EV adoption. The article says the world's 330 million SUVs emitted 1 billion tons of carbon in 2022.
- **3D-printed hotel:** Liz Lambert, ICON, and BIG are building one in Marfa, Texas, at the El Cosmico site, using ICON's Vulcan printer.
- **IoT security:** The growth in connected devices widens the attack surface, especially with hybrid work. The article recommends tailored security and SASE architecture, which bundles networking and security in a cloud-delivered service.

## April 11
- **Alibaba's Tongyi Qianwen:** The company launched a ChatGPT competitor to be integrated across its businesses. Chinese regulators proposed draft rules for generative AI, and tech figures called for a pause on training powerful AI systems. Goldman Sachs estimated AI could replace 300 million full-time jobs.
- **Application security:** The White House's National Cybersecurity Strategy points toward software makers' liability for insecure software. The article argues that responsibility shouldn't fall solely on developers.
- **Mobile cardiac telemetry:** A market report projects growth of over 12% CAGR from 2023 to 2030, with BioTelemetry, ScottCare, and Biotricity among the players.

## April 3
- **Google Cloud and Shopify:** Google's AI search and discovery tools are being integrated into Shopify's Commerce Components. Rainbow Shops saw better search accuracy. Google cites a Harris Poll finding that poor search costs retailers over $2 trillion a year.
- **Ray Kurzweil's immortality prediction:** He predicts nanobots could give humans immortality within eight years. The article says 86% of his 147 predictions were correct, a figure that is widely disputed.
- **LandVault funding:** The London metaverse startup raised more funding, reported as £2.4m and $3m (the same round in two currencies), to develop its Matera project, which makes metaverse development easier.

## Errors and doubtful claims in the original
- **"Sixth-largest country":** The article says the world's SUVs would rank as the sixth-largest emitting country. This is a comparison of the vehicles' emissions to countries, and the "1 billion tons of carbon" is probably CO₂.
- **Kurzweil:** He is a Google director of engineering, not a "former" engineer, as far as I know. His immortality timeline is highly speculative, and the 86% accuracy figure comes from his own assessments.
- **3D-printed hotel:** The "open in 2023" timeline is optimistic. Check current status before relying on it.
- **LandVault:** The £2.4m and $3m figures are inconsistent in phrasing, and the article seems to have mixed them up.

I can also write a shorter version, pull out themes like AI, cybersecurity, and green tech, or draft a LinkedIn-style post from this.

query: what are the constraint when design leachate treatement plant in North east new territories
reference:
# Constraints for Designing a Leachate Treatment Plant in the North East New Territories (NENT), Hong Kong

The NENT landfill is at Ta Kwu Ling, and the area includes the Fanling/Sheung Shui and Kwu Tung North new development areas. These constraints are drawn from general knowledge and should be checked against current project documents.

## 1. Regulatory and Statutory Constraints
- **Water Pollution Control Ordinance (WPCO)**: discharge licence limits (Technical Memorandum on Effluent Standards, TM-DSS) depend on the Water Control Zone, here likely Deep Bay or Mirs Bay/Tolo. Deep Bay is among the most stringent.
- **Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO)**: a designated project needs an EIA report and an Environmental Permit.
- **Air Pollution Control Ordinance and Noise Control Ordinance**: odour, biogas and equipment noise.
- **Waste Disposal Ordinance**: sludge and residue classification and disposal.
- **Landfill Restoration and Aftercare**: EPD's landfill gas and leachate guidance, plus long-term aftercare obligations (30+ years).
- **Buildings, Fire Services and Electrical regulations**, including hazardous area classification for biogas.

## 2. Leachate Characteristics
- High strength: COD, BOD, and ammoniacal nitrogen (often 1,000–4,000+ mg/L NH₃-N in HK landfills).
- High chloride and conductivity from the saline/mixed waste stream, which inhibits biology.
- Heavy metals and trace organics, plus recalcitrant (refractory) COD that biology cannot remove.
- **Variability** with season, waste age, and rainfall. Young leachate is high in BOD and old leachate is high in NH₃-N with low biodegradability.
- Scaling and fouling potential (Ca, Mg, Fe, carbonate), which affects pipes, membranes and aeration.

## 3. Hydrological and Climatic Constraints
- **Heavy subtropical rainfall and typhoons** cause large flow peaks, which require equalisation or storage (balancing tanks, storm lagoons).
- **Flooding risk** in low-lying NENT areas (e.g. Sheung Yue River and Ng Tung River catchments).
- High temperatures and humidity affect odour and biological kinetics.
- Wet-season dilution versus dry-season concentration.

## 4. Site and Land Constraints
- **Limited footprint**, so compact processes (MBR, SBR, MBBR) are favoured over lagoons.
- **Steep terrain and slope stability**, with geotechnical issues on a landfill platform (settlement, differential movement of the waste mass).
- Proximity to **sensitive receivers**: villages, new development areas, schools, and ecological sites.
- **Ecological sensitivity**: wetlands, fung shui woodlands, streams, and the Deep Bay catchment.
- Access roads for sludge and chemical delivery, and tanker traffic limits.
- Interface with existing landfill infrastructure (leachate collection, gas flares, liners).

## 5. Discharge and Connection Constraints
- **Sewerage connection**: discharge to the public sewer is often preferred, but the receiving works (e.g. Shek Wu Hui or Sheung Shui STW) have capacity and acceptance limits (TM Standards for discharge into foul sewers). Ammonia, COD, chloride and metals can upset the downstream plant.
- **Direct discharge to a stream** would need very high-quality effluent.
- **Trucking** to another treatment works is a backup option, with its own cost and traffic impacts.
- Chloride and salinity limits restrict reuse or discharge.

## 6. Process and Technical Constraints
- Nitrification inhibited by high NH₃-N, salinity, low C:N ratio, and toxic compounds.
- Need for **multi-stage treatment**, typically:
  - Equalisation, then biological treatment (nitrification/denitrification, MBR),
  - Then physical-chemical polishing (activated carbon, chemical oxidation, RO/nanofiltration).
- **Membrane concentrate and sludge management**, as RO generates 15–25% brine needing further handling.
- Foaming, scaling, and heavy-metal accumulation.
- Robustness to **shock loads** and to **power failure** (standby power).
- Operation over the long term as leachate quality changes during aftercare.

## 7. Environmental and Social Constraints
- **Odour control** (H₂S, NH₃, VOCs), with covered tanks and scrubbers.
- **Noise and visual impact** near rural communities.
- **Community acceptance**: the NENT landfill extension generated significant public concern.
- Construction impacts: dust, traffic, and works near ecological streams.

## 8. Economic and Operational Constraints
- Capital and operating costs, notably energy, chemicals, and membrane replacement.
- Availability of skilled operators at a remote site.
- Design life and flexibility for modular expansion.
- Sludge and concentrate disposal costs, as HK has limited disposal capacity (e.g. via the Sludge Treatment Facility, T·PARK).
- Reliability and redundancy requirements for government contracts (DBO, with performance guarantees).

## 9. Safety Constraints
- Explosive atmospheres from landfill gas near tanks.
- Confined space and H₂S exposure.
- Chemical handling (acids, caustics, oxidants, methanol/carbon source).

## Practical Design Responses
| Constraint | Typical response |
|---|---|
| Flow variability | Large balancing tank and storm storage |
| High NH₃-N | Nitrification–denitrification, MBR, or stripping |
| Refractory COD | Ozone/AOP, GAC, or RO |
| Limited land | Compact MBR/MBBR, modular units |
| Strict discharge | Sewer discharge with pretreatment, or RO polishing |
| Odour | Covered tanks, with air extraction and treatment |
| Brine | Evaporation, solidification, or recirculation (where permitted) |

**Corrections to note**
- Naguib was Egypt's first president (1953-1954), but he was forced out in November 1954 and placed under house arrest, not "sentenced." He was held until 1971.
- Nasser nationalized the canal in July 1956, after Britain had completed its troop withdrawal from the Canal Zone (agreed in 1954, completed June 1956). The US and Britain had also withdrawn their funding offer for the Aswan High Dam.
- In 1967 Egypt did not "occupy" Gaza and Sinai in a way that was new in 1948. Egypt administered Gaza (not annexed) after 1948, and Sinai was Egyptian territory. Israel captured both in 1967.

**Revised points**

1. **Muhammad Naguib (1953-1954):** Leader of the Free Officers' coup of July 1952, which overthrew King Farouk. Became the first president when the republic was declared in 1953. Clashed with Nasser over the future of civilian rule, was removed in November 1954, and was placed under house arrest. Nasser became the dominant leader and formally president in 1956.

2. **(1955) Opposition to the Baghdad Pact:** Nasser opposed this Western-backed defense alliance (Iraq, Turkey, Britain, Pakistan, Iran) as a form of neo-colonialism that split the Arab world. This pushed Egypt toward nonalignment. Nasser attended the Bandung Conference in 1955, a key step in the rise of the Non-Aligned Movement.

3. **(1955) Czech arms deal (new):** After an Israeli raid on Gaza in February 1955 and Western refusal to supply arms, Egypt made an arms deal with Czechoslovakia (the Soviet bloc). It alarmed the West and contributed to the Suez crisis.

4. **(1956) Suez Crisis:** Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company in July 1956 after the British withdrawal from the Canal Zone and the Western withdrawal of funding for the Aswan High Dam. He said canal revenues would fund the dam.

5. **(1956) Tripartite Aggression:** Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt in October-November 1956. Israel attacked Sinai, then Britain and France intervened under the pretext of separating the combatants. Military defeat was clear, but US and Soviet pressure forced the invaders to withdraw. Politically, Nasser emerged as a hero of Arab nationalism.

6. **(1956/1957) New constitution:** The 1956 constitution established a presidential system, and Nasser was confirmed as president by referendum. It granted women the vote and made Islam the state religion, but it banned political parties and concentrated power in the executive. The single party was the National Union. (Check your date: the constitution was adopted in January 1956, not 1957.)

7. **(1958-1961) United Arab Republic:** Egypt and Syria united in February 1958, with Nasser as president. Syrians came to resent Egyptian domination, and the union collapsed after a Syrian military coup in September 1961. Egypt kept the name "UAR" until 1971.

8. **Land and economic reforms (new details):** The Agrarian Reform Law of 1952 capped landholdings (initially 200 feddans) and redistributed land to peasants. After 1956-1961, Nasser nationalized foreign and major private firms, banks, and industries, adopting "Arab socialism" and five-year plans. Construction of the Aswan High Dam (begun 1960, completed 1970 with Soviet help) expanded irrigation and electricity. Results were mixed: growth in industry and education, but also bureaucracy and economic strain.

9. **(1962-1967) Yemen Civil War (new):** Egypt sent troops to support republicans against royalists in Yemen. The costly intervention drained resources and weakened the army before 1967.

10. **(1967) Six-Day War:** Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran and expelled UN peacekeepers, and Israel launched a preemptive strike in June 1967. Israel captured Sinai and the Gaza Strip (as well as the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights). Egypt suffered a devastating defeat. Nasser offered to resign but was kept in office by mass demonstrations.

11. **(1967-1970) War of Attrition and death (new):** Nasser fought a limited war of attrition along the Suez Canal and relied on Soviet support. He died of a heart attack in September 1970 and was succeeded by Anwar Sadat.

reference:
# Support for emergency and backup power in Australia

**Limits of this answer**
- I can't run live searches in this conversation, so I could not check publication dates. I can't guarantee that every item is no more than one year old, and I can't give a source under each item that I have actually just opened.
- The URLs are the official program or agency pages where you can confirm current status. Several of these programs change quickly, so check each one.
- Australia's national language is English, so no translation was needed. Search terms I would use are listed at the end.
- Items marked **(verify)** are ones where I'm less sure of the current details.

---

## 1. Federal programs

**Cheaper Home Batteries Program (since 1 July 2025)**
- It gives a discount of roughly 30% on the upfront cost of a new small-scale battery (about 5–100 kWh usable capacity). The discount is delivered as small-scale technology certificates (STCs) through the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme.
- Households, small businesses and community organisations are eligible. The battery must be installed by an accredited installer and be connected to solar.
- The discount rate and the size tiers have been revised, so check the current settings **(verify)**.
- A battery gives backup only if it is installed with a backup-capable inverter or gateway (islanding). Ask your installer, because many grid-tied systems shut down in an outage.
- Sources: https://www.dcceew.gov.au and https://www.cleanenergyregulator.gov.au

**Instant asset write-off for small business**
- Businesses with turnover under $10 million can immediately deduct eligible assets costing less than $20,000 each. This can cover generators, UPS units and batteries.
- The threshold has been extended in recent years, but it has often been legislated late. Confirm the current income-year status **(verify)**.
- Source: https://www.ato.gov.au (search "instant asset write-off")

**Disaster Ready Fund**
- This is up to $200 million a year for disaster risk reduction and resilience projects. Applicants are mostly state and territory governments, which then fund councils and community organisations. Projects can include resilient infrastructure such as community hubs with backup power.
- Source: https://nema.gov.au

**Telecommunications resilience**
- The Mobile Network Hardening Program and related programs fund batteries and generators at mobile towers in disaster-prone areas. This is relevant to telecommunications operators rather than ordinary businesses.
- Source: https://www.infrastructure.gov.au

**Regional microgrids and community energy**
- ARENA and DCCEEW run programs for regional and remote microgrids and community batteries. These are aimed at communities, councils and energy proponents, and can fund stand-alone power systems that keep supply going during outages. The program names and rounds change often **(verify)**.
- Sources: https://arena.gov.au and https://www.dcceew.gov.au

**Concessional finance**
- The Clean Energy Finance Corporation (CEFC) offers discounted finance for business energy assets such as batteries, solar and controls, mostly through banks and equipment financiers.
- Source: https://www.cefc.com.au

---

## 2. State and territory programs

| State | Program | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **NSW** | Peak Demand Reduction Scheme (PDRS) battery incentive | Gives a discount on batteries for households and small businesses, and requires the battery to be able to respond to grid signals. Source: https://www.energy.nsw.gov.au (verify the current amounts) |
| **NSW** | Reconstruction Authority and disaster recovery grants | Recovery support for businesses, primary producers and councils after declared disasters. Source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/disaster-recovery |
| **Victoria** | Solar Victoria (Solar Homes) | The battery rebate has been restructured or paused around the federal program. Check whether it is open. Source: https://www.solar.vic.gov.au **(verify)** |
| **Victoria** | Victorian Energy Upgrades | Mostly efficiency incentives. Source: https://www.energy.vic.gov.au |
| **Queensland** | Business Energy Saving and Transformation Rebates | A rebate for small and medium businesses on energy-saving equipment, up to a cap. It may cover batteries or solar, but is not aimed at backup power. Source: https://www.business.qld.gov.au **(verify)** |
| **Queensland** | QRIDA disaster assistance | Grants and concessional loans for primary producers and small businesses in declared disaster areas, which can include replacing generators or power equipment. Source: https://www.qrida.qld.gov.au |
| **Western Australia** | Residential Battery Scheme | A state rebate that works alongside the federal one. Source: https://www.wa.gov.au (search "Residential Battery Scheme") **(verify)** |
| **South Australia** | Home Battery Scheme | The earlier scheme closed. Check for any new offers. Source: https://www.energymining.sa.gov.au |

For Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory, check the state energy departments directly. I am not confident about any specific current program there. The ACT has historically run a Sustainable Household Scheme with battery loans, so look at https://www.climatechoices.act.gov.au **(verify)**.

---

## 3. Related support that is not strictly backup power
- **Life support customer protections.** Retailers and distributors must register life support customers and give outage notice. Several states offer rebates for running medical equipment, but these do not fund backup equipment. Source: https://www.aer.gov.au
- **Primary producer grants and tax.** Farm resilience, drought and disaster funding sometimes covers generators and power infrastructure. Source: https://www.agriculture.gov.au
- **Insurance and council resilience grants.** Some councils run local community resilience grants. Check your local council website.

---

## 4. Search terms to use in Australia
- "backup power rebate" or "battery backup subsidy"
- "emergency power supply grant business"
- "stand-alone power system" or "SAPS funding"
- "community resilience hub backup power grant"
- "disaster resilience grant generator"
- "business continuity energy resilience funding"
- "off-grid" or "islanding capable battery rebate"

---

## 5. What I recommend
1. Open the sources above and check the "last updated" date on each page. Discard anything older than 12 months.
2. Tell me your state, whether you are a household, business, farm or community body, and the system size. I can then narrow this down and help draft questions for installers or the program administrators.
3. If you can give me text from the program pages, I can summarise and compare them.

reference: Dan's heart skips a beat as he sees his sister Ruth walk into the bar with her friends. He hasn't seen her in a while and it's a surprise to see her there. Ruth has always been the more outgoing and adventurous of the two siblings, and Dan has always felt a little intimidated by her. But something feels off to Dan as Ruth walks over to say hello. She seems to be staring at him in a strange way, and her voice seems to take on a hypnotic quality as she speaks. Dan can't quite put his finger on what's wrong, but his senses are on high alert. "Hi Dan!" Ruth says, her voice seeming to penetrate Dan's mind. "I didn't know you were going to be here tonight. Have you been having a good time?" Dan feels a warmth spread through his body as he looks at his sister. He suddenly realizes that he's been feeling incredibly relaxed ever since he arrived at the bar, and he's not quite sure why. "I'm having a great time, thanks!" Dan replies, his voice sounding a little slurred. "What about you? You're looking really good tonight." Ruth smiles at Dan, a glint in her eye. "Thanks Dan! I'm out with some friends tonight, we're heading to a club in a little while. Do you want to come with us?" Dan feels a surge of excitement at the thought of going out with his sister and her friends. He's always felt left out of Ruth's wild nights, and the idea of finally getting to go along with her is thrilling. "I'd love to come!" Dan says eagerly. "Let me just go tell my friends and I'll be back in a minute." As Dan walks away to inform his friends of his plans, Ruth watches him go with a pleased smile on her face. She's been waiting for this moment for a long time, and she's finally going to get to show her brother just how much fun she can be.

query: 请将“At that time, regular merchant voyages linked trading centres in the Arab world, the eastern coast of Africa, India and the ‘Far East’. And this commercial world system was marked by many of the characteristics that are usually taken as indicators for the development of the capitalist world market - mature seafaring and shipbuilding, techniques of monetary transactions and exchange as well as the creation of companies in which financiers and merchants worked hand in hand. European merchants also participated in this worldwide trade. Although they played a more or less marginal role, merchants from Flanders and Champagne, Venice and Lombardy made use of these connections. They imported spices, textiles, jewels, ebony and sometimes slaves. They, by contrast, had relatively little to offer. Back then, the overall balance of trade with trading partners in the Far East was already negative, leading to a drain on silver. At the time, the world was also anything but peaceful. However, the ‘guardians’ of the trading routes guaranteed the flow of goods in exchange for toll. If from time to time the flow of goods was jeopardised, it was still possible to switch from the southern to the northern ‘silk route’ and vice versa (Abu- Lughod 1989, p. 361). And it was possible to reach India either from the Persian Gulf or the Red Sea by ship. As long as supply and demand remained intact in the three sub-systems of this trading system, world trade functioned. The decline of this world trade system was not triggered by commercial and technological backwardness or the disinterest of local rulers in trade,1 as so often suspected. But because the link was primarily a link between cities, the decline in urbanisation following the massive dying out of populations during the Black Death in the fourteenth century had a fundamental and sustained negative impact upon established relations.2 In some regions, the world trade that was to start out from Europe in the sixteenth century took up where earlier trading relations had left off.3 But on the whole, it was a new system. Because merchants of various origins were no longer prepared to allow one another to make use of the infrastructures of the trading routes of their region without hindrance, the age of monopolies had been born, and thus that of armed competition (as shown by Braudel 1979/1986). That competition was manifest in sea battles and raids on trading bases. And it was this practice of armed competition for trading monopolies which distinguished the world trade emerging from the end of the fifteenth century onwards from the world trade of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. If there had been attacks on the property and possibly even the lives of traders earlier, the era of armed trade first came to prevail systematically when European merchant warriors sailed the world’s seas. According to Kirti N. Chaudhuri, who conducted research on the development of trade and culture in the region of the Indian Ocean up until 1750, it is less the new development in trade relations that required explanation than the development of thoroughly armed trade (1985, p. 14). Armed trade emerged from governmental practice in the countries of origin of the merchant warriors, where in early modernity one European ruler after the other developed a practice of conferring privileges. Trading companies hoped that by acquiring a privilege, they would have the support of rulers in eliminating competition, and this was only possible if the prince announced his claim over a trading monopoly in a certain region of the world. In exchange for such privileges, the princes had themselves paid and awarded shares of expected profits. Even if the profits were not always forthcoming, appropriation through trade was thus closely tied to appropriation by princes, and thus to the use of violence. The increased presence of Europeans furthered the decline in long-term trading relations between partners. Instead, violence was often employed to earn short-term and often predatory profits. Consequently, merchants aimed at establishing trading bases that were secured and defended with the use of arms. Thus, the growing participation of European merchant warriors altered the practice of international trade.4 Robbery and Regulations While most merchants acting overseas aimed at gaining acceptance in their mother countries as members of the upper and possibly even aristocratic classes, they were less troubled by their reputation when they were overseas. Wherever they saw an opportunity, they appropriated the riches of peoples when they were overseas without bothering with the niceties of trade. An early example of this practice is to be seen in the first Iberian adventurers in South America. When they realised that Amerindians did not have the kind of merchandise they had hoped for, they plundered whatever seemed worth plundering. But they especially went for gold. ‘They were as greedy for gold as hungry pigs’, Aztecs are reported to have said of them.5 In the early stage of the ‘world market’ which had its origins in Europe, European merchant warriors not only plundered what they found abroad. Instead, wherever it appeared possible, they found shortcuts for the process of appropriation by attacking the ships loaded by their European competitors. Historical accounts read like reports on fights between bands of robbers.6 And that is precisely what they were.7 But because equipping ships was costly and princes wanted their share of the booty, many of those who participated in raids on the high seas were commissioned by or at least acted with the tacit assent of the princes of the mother countries. Even if these silent or even official partners in raids on the high seas thought the violent appropriation of wealth in every part of the world was par-ticularly desirable, they had to take account of the potential negative effects on their rule. In other words, robbing one’s European competitors had to bear at least the appearance of legitimacy. Just as on land, legitimacy for such raids was created by claiming territorial rights over parts of the seas. Much later the argument was put forward to do away with such claims because territorial rights over certain regions of the seas could not really be successfully defended. But that had not really been the point throughout the period in which such arguments were put forward as valid. For whosoever claimed territorial rights over an entire region of the sea gave himself the right to impound any ship found in the region without requiring the permission of whoever exercised sovereign jurisdiction over the vessel, to confiscate its cargo and to pass sentence on its crew as pirates. There was no court in which the legality of such a procedure could be challenged; therefore, the publication of a claim to the dominion over a certain part of the world seas included the claim to decide what was right and wrong in that territory. Letus start out by following, if only very roughly, the carving up of the world’s seas in territories. This began in 1493 when Columbus and his crew returned from their first major voyage. It had started the great race for wealth overseas. Initially, only the Crowns of Spain and Portugal seemed to have the prospect of competing successfully in this race. In order to not destabilise their rule in Europe, both powers turned to the Pope so that he could carve up the New World for them. The fact that the demarcation line chosen was changed again the following year shows clearly that negotiations prior to the conclusion of the treaty had been tough.8 Be that as it may, the ‘world’ outside Europe was split up between Spain and Portugal on 7 June 1494 under the aegis of Pope Alexander vi in the Treaty of Tordesillas. Whatever was to be found further than 370 nautical miles west of the Cape Verde Islands went to the Kingdom of Spain, while everything to the east of this imaginary line belonged to the Kingdom of Portugal. Since the end of the fifteenth century, the high sea between Europe and the Americas had thus been formally broken up into territories.9 To be precise, the Pope did not determine which part of the New World both kingdoms could rightly appropriate, but merely distributed territories in which they were allowed to do missionary work.10 Of course, this specific detail played no role in practice. Further demarcations followed. In 1526, the Treaty of Zaragoza established how the Pacific was split up. The so-called Moluccas antemeridian corresponded to today’s 135th meridian. It is possible that these lines kept Portuguese and Spanish ships from entering each other’s territories in the high seas, as laid down in the treaty, but for the French corsairs and English ‘discoverers’ sailing the seas for booty from the sixteenth century onwards, these treaties only consisted of a risk if they were defeated on the seas. To reduce this risk and thereby enhance their chances of getting a share of said booty, the rulers of the new sea powers challenged the legitimacy of the lines and demanded that their subjects should have the right to sail through the sea regions claimed by Portugal and Spain.n In Câteau-Cambrésis, negotiations were conducted for a peace treaty between Spain and France in 1559.12 It was said that there had been an additional, oral agreement amending the published text of the treaty. In any case, it was reported time and again that the peace treaty was limited to Europe and that armed conflicts beyond this ‘line of friendship’ would not be interpreted as a breach of the treaty. Although the issue of whether the treaty had this additional clause alongside the official version is still open to debate/3 it played a considerable role in academic debates over the past decades, triggered by a publication by Carl Schmitt in 1950, which in turn referred to a publication by Gustav Adolf Rein from 1930. According to Schmitt, bracketing out an area of combat outside Europe served war in Europe (1950, p. 66).14 More recent research on the treaty negotiations have shown that Spain offered to reduce its claim on territories, hitherto based on the Treaty of Tordesillas. But ultimately, Spain did not give up its claims (Kempe 2010, p. 57). They continued to apply to everyone who continued to run the risk of being attacked as pirates when violating the maritime territory to which Spain laid claim.”翻译为中文

当时,定期的商船航行把阿拉伯世界、非洲东海岸、印度和“远东”的贸易中心连接在一起。这一商业世界体系具有许多通常被视为资本主义世界市场发展标志的特征:成熟的航海与造船业、货币交易与汇兑技术,以及金融家与商人携手合作的公司的创立。欧洲商人也参与了这种世界范围的贸易。尽管他们的角色或多或少处于边缘,来自佛兰德和香槟、威尼斯和伦巴第的商人仍利用了这些联系。他们进口香料、纺织品、珠宝、乌木,有时还有奴隶,而他们自己能提供的东西相对很少。当时,与远东贸易伙伴之间的总体贸易差额已经是逆差,导致白银外流。那时的世界也绝非和平。不过,贸易路线的“守护者”以收取通行费为条件保障货物流通。如果货物流通时而受到威胁,仍可以从南线“丝绸之路”转到北线,反之亦然(Abu-Lughod 1989,第361页)。而且,无论从波斯湾还是红海,都可以乘船抵达印度。只要这一贸易体系的三个子系统中的供给与需求保持完好,世界贸易就能运转。

这一世界贸易体系的衰落,并不像人们常常猜测的那样,是由商业和技术上的落后,或当地统治者对贸易的漠不关心所引发的。^1 由于这种联系主要是城市之间的联系,十四世纪黑死病造成人口大量死亡之后的城市化衰退,对既有的关系产生了根本而持久的负面影响。^2 在某些地区,十六世纪从欧洲出发的世界贸易接续了早先贸易关系中断之处。^3 但总体而言,这是一个全新的体系。由于来自不同地方的商人不再愿意彼此无阻碍地使用对方所在地区贸易路线的基础设施,垄断的时代便诞生了,随之而来的是武装竞争的时代(如布罗代尔 1979/1986 所示)。这种竞争表现为海战和对贸易据点的袭击。正是这种为争夺贸易垄断而进行武装竞争的做法,使十五世纪末以来兴起的世界贸易有别于十三、十四世纪的世界贸易。此前虽也有针对商人财产乃至生命的攻击,但武装贸易系统性地占据主导,是从欧洲商人武士航行于世界海洋时才开始的。

研究1750年以前印度洋地区贸易与文化发展的基尔蒂·N·乔杜里认为,需要解释的与其说是贸易关系中的新发展,不如说是彻底武装化的贸易的发展(1985,第14页)。武装贸易源于商人武士母国的统治实践:在近代早期,欧洲的统治者一个接一个地发展出授予特许权的做法。贸易公司希望通过获得特许权得到君主的支持来消除竞争,而这只有在君主宣布对世界某一地区的贸易垄断拥有主张时才可能。作为授予特许权的回报,君主让人向自己付款,并分得预期利润的份额。即便利润并不总能到手,通过贸易进行的占取也因此与君主的占取、从而与暴力的使用紧密相连。欧洲人的更多到来加速了贸易伙伴之间长期贸易关系的衰落。取而代之的是,人们常常使用暴力来获取短期的、往往是掠夺性的利润。因此,商人们力求建立用武力保障和防卫的贸易据点。这样,欧洲商人武士的日益参与改变了国际贸易的实践。^4

**抢劫与规则**

虽然大多数海外活动的商人力图在母国被接纳为上层乃至贵族阶层的成员,但身在海外时,他们并不太在意自己的名声。只要看到机会,他们就占取当地人民的财富,而不顾贸易的体面。这种做法的一个早期例子,见于最初来到南美洲的伊比利亚冒险者。当他们意识到美洲印第安人并没有他们所期望的那种商品时,便掠夺一切看似值得掠夺的东西,尤其是黄金。据说阿兹特克人曾这样评价他们:“他们对黄金的贪婪,就像饥饿的猪。”^5

在起源于欧洲的“世界市场”的早期阶段,欧洲商人武士不仅掠夺在海外发现的东西。只要看起来可能,他们还通过攻击欧洲竞争对手装满货物的船只,为占取过程找到捷径。历史记载读起来就像关于强盗团伙之间争斗的报道。^6 而他们恰恰就是如此。^7 但由于装备船只花费高昂,君主们又想分得战利品,许多参与公海劫掠的人是受母国君主委托,或至少是在其默许下行动的。即使这些沉默的乃至正式的公海劫掠伙伴认为,在世界各地以暴力占取财富特别可取,他们也必须顾及这对其统治可能产生的负面影响。换言之,劫掠欧洲竞争对手至少要带有合法性的外观。正如在陆地上一样,此类劫掠的合法性是通过对部分海域主张领土权利而创造出来的。很久以后,有人提出取消这类主张,理由是对某些海域的领土权利其实无法成功捍卫。但在这类论据被视为有效的整个时期,这并非问题的关键。因为凡是对整片海域主张领土权利的人,就赋予了自己这样的权利:扣押在该海域发现的任何船只,而无需获得对该船行使主权管辖者的许可;没收其货物;并将船员作为海盗加以判决。没有任何法庭可以对这种做法的合法性提出质疑;因此,宣布对世界海洋某一部分拥有支配权,就包含了在该领域决定是非对错的主张。

让我们先大致追溯一下世界海洋被划分为各个领地的过程。这始于1493年,哥伦布及其船员结束首次重大航行归来之时。那次航行开启了海外财富的大竞赛。最初,似乎只有西班牙和葡萄牙两国王室有望在这场竞赛中成功竞争。为了不动摇它们在欧洲的统治,两国都求助于教皇,请他为它们瓜分新世界。次年所选定的分界线又被更改,这清楚地表明条约缔结之前的谈判十分艰难。^8 无论如何,1494年6月7日,在教皇亚历山大六世的主持下,欧洲以外的“世界”通过《托尔德西里亚斯条约》在西班牙和葡萄牙之间被瓜分。在佛得角群岛以西370海里之外所发现的一切归西班牙王国,而这条假想线以东的一切则属于葡萄牙王国。因此,自十五世纪末以来,欧洲与美洲之间的公海就已被正式划分为若干领地。^9 确切地说,教皇并未确定两个王国可以正当占取新世界的哪一部分,而只是分配了它们可以在其中传教的区域。^10 当然,这一具体细节在实践中毫无作用。

随后又有进一步的划界。1526年,《萨拉戈萨条约》确定了太平洋如何划分。所谓摩鹿加反子午线相当于今天的东经135度。这些界线也许确实如条约所规定的那样,使葡萄牙和西班牙的船只不进入对方在公海中的领地,但对于自十六世纪起为劫掠而航行于海上的法国私掠船和英国“发现者”来说,这些条约只有在他们在海上被击败时才构成风险。为了降低这种风险,从而增加分得战利品的机会,新兴海上强国的统治者对这些界线的合法性提出质疑,并要求其臣民有权通过葡萄牙和西班牙所主张的海域航行。^11

1559年,西班牙与法国在卡托-康布雷西就和平条约进行谈判。^12 据说,除公布的条约文本外,还有一项口头的补充协议。无论如何,人们一再报道说,该和平条约仅限于欧洲,在这条“友好线”之外的武装冲突不会被解释为违反条约。尽管条约除正式文本外是否确有这一附加条款仍有争议,^13 但它在过去几十年的学术争论中扮演了重要角色,这些争论由卡尔·施米特1950年的一部著作引发,而该著作又参考了古斯塔夫·阿道夫·莱因1930年的一部著作。按照施米特的说法,把欧洲以外的一片区域排除在战场之外,是服务于欧洲的战争的(1950,第66页)。^14 对条约谈判的较新研究表明,西班牙曾提出缩减其此前基于《托尔德西里亚斯条约》的领土主张。但最终,西班牙并未放弃其主张(Kempe 2010,第57页)。这些主张继续适用于所有冒险侵入西班牙所主张海域的人,他们始终面临被当作海盗攻击的风险。

请将“At that time, regular merchant voyages linked trading centres in the Arab world, the eastern coast of Africa, India and the ‘Far East’. And this commercial world system was marked by many of the characteristics that are usually taken as indicators for the development of the capitalist world market - mature seafaring and shipbuilding, techniques of monetary transactions and exchange as well as the creation of companies in which financiers and merchants worked hand in hand. European merchants also participated in this worldwide trade. Although they played a more or less marginal role, merchants from [REDACTED] and [REDACTED], [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] made use of these connections. They imported spices, textiles, jewels, ebony and sometimes slaves. They, by contrast, had relatively little to offer. Back then, the overall balance of trade with trading partners in the Far East was already negative, leading to a drain on silver. At the time, the world was also anything but peaceful. However, the ‘guardians’ of the trading routes guaranteed the flow of goods in exchange for toll. If from time to time the flow of goods was jeopardised, it was still possible to switch from the southern to the northern ‘silk route’ and vice versa ([REDACTED] [REDACTED], p. 361). And it was possible to reach India either from the Persian Gulf or the Red Sea by ship. As long as supply and demand remained intact in the three sub-systems of this trading system, world trade functioned. The decline of this world trade system was not triggered by commercial and technological backwardness or the disinterest of local rulers in trade,1 as so often suspected. But because the link was primarily a link between cities, the decline in urbanisation following the massive dying out of populations during the Black Death in the fourteenth century had a fundamental and sustained negative impact upon established relations.2 In some regions, the world trade that was to start out from Europe in the sixteenth century took up where earlier trading relations had left off.3 But on the whole, it was a new system. Because merchants of various origins were no longer prepared to allow one another to make use of the infrastructures of the trading routes of their region without hindrance, the age of monopolies had been born, and thus that of armed competition (as shown by [REDACTED] [REDACTED]/[REDACTED]). That competition was manifest in sea battles and raids on trading bases. And it was this practice of armed competition for trading monopolies which distinguished the world trade emerging from the end of the fifteenth century onwards from the world trade of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. If there had been attacks on the property and possibly even the lives of traders earlier, the era of armed trade first came to prevail systematically when European merchant warriors sailed the world’s seas. According to [REDACTED] N. [REDACTED], who conducted research on the development of trade and culture in the region of the Indian Ocean up until 1750, it is less the new development in trade relations that required explanation than the development of thoroughly armed trade. (1985, p. 14). Armed trade emerged from governmental practice in the countries of origin of the merchant warriors, where in early modernity one European ruler after the other developed a practice of conferring privileges. Trading companies hoped that by acquiring a privilege, they would have the support of rulers in eliminating competition, and this was only possible if the prince announced his claim over a trading monopoly in a certain region of the world. In exchange for such privileges, the princes had themselves paid and awarded shares of expected profits. Even if the profits were not always forthcoming, appropriation through trade was thus closely tied to appropriation by princes, and thus to the use of violence. The increased presence of Europeans furthered the decline in long-term trading relations between partners. Instead, violence was often employed to earn short-term and often predatory profits. Consequently, merchants aimed at establishing trading bases that were secured and defended with the use of arms. Thus, the growing participation of European merchant warriors altered the practice of international trade.4 Robbery and Regulations While most merchants acting overseas aimed at gaining acceptance in their mother countries as members of the upper and possibly even aristocratic classes, they were less troubled by their reputation when they were overseas. Wherever they saw an opportunity, they appropriated the riches of peoples when they were overseas without bothering with the niceties of trade. An early example of this practice is to be seen in the first Iberian adventurers in South America. When they realised that Amerindians did not have the kind of merchandise they had hoped for, they plundered whatever seemed worth plundering. But they especially went for gold. ‘They were as greedy for gold as hungry pigs’, Aztecs are reported to have said of them.5 In the early stage of the ‘world market’ which had its origins in Europe, European merchant warriors not only plundered what they found abroad. Instead, wherever it appeared possible, they found shortcuts for the process of appropriation by attacking the ships loaded by their European competitors. Historical accounts read like reports on fights between bands of robbers.6 And that is precisely what they were.7 But because equipping ships was costly and princes wanted their share of the booty, many of those who participated in raids on the high seas were commissioned by or at least acted with the tacit assent of the princes of the mother countries. Even if these silent or even official partners in raids on the high seas thought the violent appropriation of wealth in every part of the world was par-ticularly desirable, they had to take account of the potential negative effects on their rule. In other words, robbing one’s European competitors had to bear at least the appearance of legitimacy. Just as on land, legitimacy for such raids was created by claiming territorial rights over parts of the seas. Much later the argument was put forward to do away with such claims because territorial rights over certain regions of the seas could not really be successfully defended. But that had not really been the point throughout the period in which such arguments were put forward as valid. For whosoever claimed territorial rights over an entire region of the sea gave himself the right to impound any ship found in the region without requiring the permission of whoever exercised sovereign jurisdiction over the vessel, to confiscate its cargo and to pass sentence on its crew as pirates. There was no court in which the legality of such a procedure could be challenged; therefore, the publication of a claim to the dominion over a certain part of the world seas included the claim to decide what was right and wrong in that territory. Let us start out by following, if only very roughly, the carving up of the world’s seas in territories. This began in 1493 when Columbus and his crew returned from their first major voyage. It had started the great race for wealth overseas. Initially, only the Crowns of [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] seemed to have the prospect of competing successfully in this race. In order to not destabilise their rule in Europe, both powers turned to the Pope so that he could carve up the New World for them. The fact that the demarcation line chosen was changed again the following year shows clearly that negotiations prior to the conclusion of the treaty had been tough.8 Be that as it may, the ‘world’ outside Europe was split up between [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] on 7 June 1494 under the aegis of Pope Alexander vi in the Treaty of [REDACTED]. Whatever was to be found further than 370 nautical miles west of the Cape Verde Islands went to the Kingdom of [REDACTED], while everything to the east of this imaginary line belonged to the Kingdom of [REDACTED]. Since the end of the fifteenth century, the high sea between Europe and the Americas had thus been formally broken up into territories.9 To be precise, the Pope did not determine which part of the New World both kingdoms could rightly appropriate, but merely distributed territories in which they were allowed to do missionary work.10 Of course, this specific detail played no role in practice. Further demarcations followed. In 1526, the Treaty of [REDACTED] established how the Pacific was split up. The so-called Moluccas antemeridian corresponded to today’s 135th meridian. It is possible that these lines kept Portuguese and Spanish ships from entering each other’s territories in the high seas, as laid down in the treaty, but for the French corsairs and English ‘discoverers’ sailing the seas for booty from the sixteenth century onwards, these treaties only consisted of a risk if they were defeated on the seas. To reduce this risk and thereby enhance their chances of getting a share of said booty, the rulers of the new sea powers challenged the legitimacy of the lines and demanded that their subjects should have the right to sail through the sea regions claimed by [REDACTED] and [REDACTED].n In [REDACTED], negotiations were conducted for a peace treaty between [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] in 1559.12 It was said that there had been an additional, oral agreement amending the published text of the treaty. In any case, it was reported time and again that the peace treaty was limited to Europe and that armed conflicts beyond this ‘line of friendship’ would not be interpreted as a breach of the treaty. Although the issue of whether the treaty had this additional clause alongside the official version is still open to debate/3 it played a considerable role in academic debates over the past decades, triggered by a publication by [REDACTED] in 1950, which in turn referred to a publication by [REDACTED] from 1930. According to [REDACTED], bracketing out an area of combat outside Europe served war in Europe (1950, p. 66).14 More recent research on the treaty negotiations have shown that [REDACTED] offered to reduce its claim on territories, hitherto based on the Treaty of [REDACTED]. But ultimately, [REDACTED] did not give up its claims (Kempe 2010, p. 57). They continued to apply to everyone who continued to run the risk of being attacked as pirates when violating the maritime territory to which [REDACTED] laid claim.”

meta.pupa_reference: 在那个时期，定期的商船航行连接着阿拉伯世界、非洲东海岸、印度以及“远东”的贸易中心。这个商业世界体系被许多通常被视为资本主义世界市场发展指标的特征所标记——成熟的航海和造船技术、货币交易和交换技术以及金融家和商人合作的公司的创建。 欧洲商人也参与了这一全球贸易。尽管他们扮演了或多或少边缘性的角色，来自佛兰德、香槟、威尼斯和伦巴第的商人利用了这些联系。他们进口香料、纺织品、珠宝、乌木，有时也有奴隶。与之相比，他们几乎没有什么可以提供的。当时，与远东贸易伙伴的总体贸易平衡已经是负的，导致银行流失。 当时，世界也远非和平。然而，贸易路线的“守护者”通过收取过路费来保证货物的流通。如果货物流动偶尔受到威胁，仍然可以从南方的“丝绸之路”切换到北方，反之亦然（Abu-Lughod 1989，第361页）。而且还可以从波斯湾或红海乘船抵达印度。只要这个贸易系统的三个子系统中的供需保持完整，世界贸易就能运作。这个世界贸易体系的衰退并非由商业和技术的落后或地方统治者对贸易的不感兴趣触发，正如人们经常怀疑的那样。但是因为这个联系主要是城市之间的联系，因此14世纪黑死病期间人口的大量死亡对城市化的下降造成了根本性和持续的负面影响，对既有关系产生了根本性和持续的负面影响。 在某些地区，16世纪从欧洲开始的世界贸易接替了之前的贸易关系。但总体上，它是一个新系统。因为来自不同来源的商人不再愿意彼此无障碍地使用彼此地区的贸易路线的基础设施，垄断时代已经诞生，因此武装竞争时代（如Braudel 1979/1986所示）已经诞生。这种竞争表现在海上战斗和对贸易基地的袭击上。正是这种对贸易垄断权的武装竞争实践，区别于13和14世纪的世界贸易，标志着从15世纪末开始出现的世界贸易。 如果说之前对贸易商的财产甚至生命的攻击也曾存在，当欧洲的商业战士航行世界各海时，武装贸易的时代才首次系统性地盛行。根据Kirti N. Chaudhuri的研究，他研究了直到1750年印度洋地区贸易和文化的发展，不是贸易关系的新发展需要解释，而是彻底的武装贸易的发展（1985年，第14页）。 武装贸易源于商业战士的原籍国的政府实践，在那里，一个又一个的欧洲统治者在早期现代性逐渐形成了授予权利的实践。贸易公司希望通过获得特权，他们将得到统治者的支持，以消除竞争，这只有在某地区的世界宣布对贸易垄断的主张时才可能实现。为了获得这样的特权，王侯们让自己得到了报酬，并获得了预期利润的份额。即使利润并不总是如期而至，通过贸易的占有从而与王侯的占有紧密联系起来，因此与使用暴力紧密联系起来。 欧洲人的增加促进了长期贸易关系的下降。相反，往往使用暴力来获得短期和经常是掠夺性的利润。因此，商人们旨在建立用武器保护和防御的贸易基地。因此，欧洲商业战士的日益参与改变了国际贸易的实践。 掠夺与规范 虽然大多数在海外行事的商人都希望在母国被接纳为上层甚至可能是贵族阶层的成员，但当他们在海外时，他们对自己的声誉不太在意。在他们看到机会的地方，他们不顾贸易的规矩，侵占了当地人民的财富。 这种做法的一个早期例子可以在南美的第一批伊比利亚冒险家中看到。当他们意识到美洲土著没有他们希望的那种商品时，他们掠夺了看似值得掠夺的一切。但他们尤其追求黄金。“他们像饥饿的猪一样渴望黄金”，据说阿兹特克人这样说过他们。 在欧洲起源的“世界市场”的早期阶段，欧洲的商业战士不仅掠夺了他们在国外发现的东西。相反，只要有可能，他们就通过攻击欧洲竞争对手装载的船只，为占有过程找到捷径。历史记录读起来就像是抢劫团伙之间战斗的报道。而这正是它们的本质。 但是因为装备船只成本高昂，王侯们想要分得战利品的份额，许多参与高海上突袭的人士是受到母国王侯的委托，或至少是在王侯的默许下行动的。即使这些在高海上突袭中的沉默或官方合作者认为在世界每个角落通过暴力占有财富是特别理想的，他们也必须考虑到其对统治的潜在负面影响。换句话说，抢劫欧洲竞争对手至少必须具有合法性的外观。就像在陆地上一样，通过声称对海域部分地区的领土权来为这种突袭创造合法性。直到很久以后，才提出废除这种主张的论点，因为海域的某些地区的领土权真的无法成功维护。但这并不是在提出这些论点为有效期间的真正要点。 无论谁宣称对整个海域地区的领土权，给了自己在该区域发现的任何船只进行扣押的权力，无需获得对船只行使主权管辖权的人的许可，没收其货物并对其船员判定为海盗的权力。没有法院可以挑战这种程序的合法性；因此，宣称对世界海域某个部分拥有统治权的声明包括了决定该领土上什么是对与错的权力。 让我们开始跟踪，即使非常粗略地，对世界海域进行领土划分。这始于1493年，当哥伦布和他的船员从他们的第一次大航行返回时。这开启了海外财富的伟大竞赛。最初，只有西班牙和葡萄牙的王室似乎有成功竞争的前景。为了不破坏他们在欧洲的统治，两国都向教皇求助，以便他为他们划分新世界。明显的是，次年选择的分界线再次被改变，清楚地表明先前的条约谈判非常艰难。但无论如何，在教皇亚历山大六世的庇护下，1494年6月7日签订了托尔德西拉斯条约，将“世界”以外的欧洲分割给了西班牙和葡萄牙。凡是从佛得角群岛向西370海里以外的区域归西班牙王国所有，而这条想象线东侧的一切都属于葡萄牙王国。从15世纪末开始，欧洲与美洲之间的公海因此被正式划分成了领土。要精确地说，教皇并未决定两个王国可以正当地占有新世界的哪个部分，而仅仅是分配了他们被允许进行传教工作的领土。当然，这个具体细节在实践中没有任何作用。 进一步的领土划分随之而来。1526年的萨拉戈萨条约确定了太平洋的分割。所谓的摩鹿加群岛对跖点对应今天的第135经线。可能这些线阻止了葡萄牙和西班牙的船只进入高海上条约中规定的彼此领土，但对于从16世纪开始在海上寻找战利品的法国私掠船和英国“探险家”来说，这些条约只有在他们在海上被击败时才构成风险。 为了减少这种风险，从而增加获取战利品的机会，新的海上大国的统治者挑战了这些线的合法性，并要求他们的臣民有权通过葡萄牙和西班牙声称的海域。在1559年西班牙和法国之间为了一项和平条约进行的卡托-坎布雷西斯谈判中，据说有一个额外的口头协议修订了公布的条约文本。无论如何，一直有报道称和平条约仅限于欧洲，超出这个“友谊线”的武装冲突不会被解释为违反条约。虽然关于条约是否有这样一个额外的条款与官方版本并行的问题仍然存在争议，但在过去几十年的学术辩论中，这在很大程度上是由卡尔·施密特于1950年发表的出版物引发的，该出版物又参考了古斯塔夫·阿道夫·莱因1930年的出版物。根据施密特的说法，在欧洲之外排除一个战斗区域有助于欧洲的战争（1950年，第66页）。近期关于条约谈判的研究表明，西班牙提出减少其基于托尔德西拉斯条约的领土要求。但最终，西班牙并未放弃其主张。它们继续适用于所有继续冒着被攻击为海盗风险的人，当他们侵犯西班牙声称的海域领土时。

reference:
# History of Cholera in Iraq

## Background: The Regional Context
Cholera is endemic to the Ganges Delta in South Asia, and Iraq's position along pilgrimage routes, trade corridors, and the Tigris-Euphrates river system made it an early and recurring entry point into the Middle East.

## 19th Century: The Pandemics Arrive

**First pandemic (1817–1824):** Cholera spread from India through the Persian Gulf. Basra was affected around 1821, and the disease moved up toward Baghdad and beyond.

**Second pandemic (1826–1837):** Baghdad was hit hard in 1831. The outbreak, combined with a catastrophic Tigris flood and plague the same year, devastated the city. Estimates suggest the population fell dramatically, and the Mamluk rule of Dawud Pasha was seriously weakened.

**Later 19th-century waves:** Iraq saw repeated outbreaks (e.g., the 1846–47, 1850s, 1860s, and 1889–90 periods). The Shia holy cities of Karbala and Najaf, which draw large numbers of pilgrims (including from Iran and India), were important nodes in transmitting cholera across the region. This led to international concern and early efforts at quarantine, including the Ottoman and international sanitary councils.

## Early 20th Century
- **British Mandate era (1920s–1932):** British administrators established public health services and quarantine measures, partly aimed at controlling disease entering via the Gulf and from Iran. Cholera outbreaks still occurred periodically, such as in the 1920s.
- Quarantine and vaccination campaigns became more standard, particularly around pilgrimage seasons.

## Mid-20th Century
- **Seventh pandemic (began 1961):** The El Tor biotype spread from Indonesia across Asia. It reached Iraq in the early 1960s, with outbreaks around 1965–66 and later in the 1970s.
- Cholera was sometimes under-reported in this era, as governments in the region worried about trade and travel restrictions.

## Late 20th Century
- Improved water and sanitation infrastructure in the 1970s–80s reduced some risk.
- **1991 Gulf War and sanctions:** Bombing damaged water treatment, sewage, and electrical systems. Sanctions limited repairs and supplies like chlorine. Waterborne diseases, including cholera, rose in the 1990s, though reliable data are limited.

## 21st Century
- **2007–2008:** A significant outbreak began in northern Iraq (Sulaymaniyah and Kirkuk) in August 2007, spreading to other provinces, with thousands of confirmed cases. Drought, poor water quality, and damaged infrastructure were contributing factors.
- **2012–2015:** Smaller outbreaks occurred. In 2015, an outbreak began in Baghdad and spread widely (to many provinces) amid conflict and displacement linked to ISIS, with displaced-persons camps being a major concern. Several thousand cases were reported.
- **2022:** Iraq reported cholera again, with outbreaks beginning in the north (Sulaymaniyah) and spreading, alongside regional outbreaks in Syria and Lebanon. Drivers included drought, low river levels, contaminated water, and aging infrastructure.
- **2023–present:** Water scarcity, climate change, upstream dams, and salinity problems (especially in Basra) continue to raise risk, along with periodic localized outbreaks and concerns about water quality.

## Recurring Risk Factors
- Damaged or aging water and sanitation systems
- Conflict, displacement, and crowded camps
- Mass gatherings (e.g., Arbaeen pilgrimage to Karbala)
- Drought and declining river quality
- Regional transmission via Iran, Syria, and the Gulf

## Caveat
Historical case counts and death tolls, especially for the 19th century, are estimates and vary by source. If you'd like, I can go deeper into a particular period (e.g., the 1831 Baghdad outbreak or the 2007 epidemic) or suggest sources.

query: Dream Theater Co. declares cash dividends of P10 per share on March 1, 20x1, to shareholders of record as of March 15, for distribution on March 20. How much dividend income should John Myung recognize?
reference:
The problem as stated doesn't say how many shares John Myung owns, so the answer has to be expressed per share, with a note on when the income is recognized.

**Timing of recognition**

Under PFRS 9 / IFRS 9, an investor recognizes dividend income when its right to receive payment is established. That is the **declaration date**, March 1, 20x1, not the record date or the payment date. The investor's accounting entries are:

- **March 1 (declaration):** Dr. Dividends receivable, Cr. Dividend income
- **March 15 (record date):** no entry
- **March 20 (payment):** Dr. Cash, Cr. Dividends receivable

**Amount**

Dividend income = P10 × number of shares owned.

For example, if John Myung owned 1,000 shares, he would recognize P10,000 of dividend income on March 1, 20x1.

**Answer:** P10 per share, recognized on the declaration date of March 1, 20x1 (total = P10 × shares held).

One caveat: if he buys the shares after the declaration but before the record date, the purchase price already includes the dividend, so the dividend is treated as a reduction of the investment cost rather than as income. This doesn't apply if he was already a holder on March 1.

## Как исправить

### 1. Найти и завершить процесс, занявший порт

**Windows (cmd/PowerShell):**
```bash
netstat -ano | findstr :18107
taskkill /PID <PID> /F
```
PID будет в последнем столбце вывода первой команды.

**Linux / macOS:**
```bash
lsof -i :18107
kill -9 <PID>
```
или одной командой:
```bash
kill -9 $(lsof -t -i:18107)
```

### 2. Проверить IntelliJ IDEA
Часто причина в том, что приложение уже запущено:
- Откройте вкладки **Run / Services** и остановите все запущенные экземпляры (красный квадрат).
- Проверьте, нет ли «зависшего» Java-процесса в диспетчере задач (`java.exe`) или через `jps`.
- Убедитесь, что у вас не запущены две конфигурации одного приложения.

### 3. Сменить порт
Если освободить порт нельзя, измените его:

**application.properties**
```properties
server.port=8081
```

**application.yml**
```yaml
server:
  port: 8081
```

Либо через параметр запуска: `--server.port=8081` или VM option `-Dserver.port=8081`.

### 4. Случайный свободный порт (например, для тестов)
```properties
server.port=0
```

`Disconnected from the target VM...` и `exit code 1` — это просто следствие: приложение аварийно завершилось, и отладчик отключился. Настоящая причина только в первой строке про занятый порт.

reference:
Похоже, речь про SNMPv3 с аутентификацией MD5 и шифрованием DES (уровень authPriv). Команда:

```bash
snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u initi_user -a MD5 -A d2J3BgtYdB2 -x DES -X d2J3BgtYdB2 10.2.35.2
```

**Параметры:**
- `-v3`: версия SNMP
- `-l authPriv`: уровень безопасности (аутентификация и шифрование)
- `-u initi_user`: имя пользователя
- `-a MD5`: протокол аутентификации
- `-A`: пароль аутентификации
- `-x DES`: протокол шифрования
- `-X`: пароль шифрования

**Полезные дополнения:**

Указать конкретную ветку OID (например, system):
```bash
snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u initi_user -a MD5 -A d2J3BgtYdB2 -x DES -X d2J3BgtYdB2 10.2.35.2 1.3.6.1.2.1.1
```

Если нужен контекст или нестандартный порт:
```bash
snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u initi_user -a MD5 -A d2J3BgtYdB2 -x DES -X d2J3BgtYdB2 -n "" 10.2.35.2:161
```

**Замечания:**
- Если вы имели в виду, что `d2J3BgtYdB2` повторяется дважды, потому что пароли аутентификации и шифрования одинаковы, то команда выше верна.
- Если в новых версиях net-snmp DES не работает (отключен при сборке), попробуйте добавить `-v3` с `-x AES`, если устройство поддерживает, либо используйте сборку с поддержкой DES.
- Пароли в командной строке видны в истории и в списке процессов. Для безопасности можно вынести их в `~/.snmp/snmp.conf`:
  ```
  defSecurityName initi_user
  defAuthType MD5
  defAuthPassphrase d2J3BgtYdB2
  defPrivType DES
  defPrivPassphrase d2J3BgtYdB2
  defSecurityLevel authPriv
  ```
  После этого достаточно: `snmpwalk -v3 10.2.35.2`

However, here are three possible symptoms and explanations for their occurrence: 1. Headaches: Headaches are a prevalent symptom of brain tumors. The tumor can cause increased pressure within the skull, leading to chronic or worsening headaches. Tumors can also disrupt the normal flow of cerebrospinal fluid, leading to further pressure buildup and resulting in headaches. Additionally, as the tumor grows, it can compress or invade surrounding tissues, triggering pain signals. 2. Seizures: Brain tumors can irritate or disrupt the normal electrical activity in the brain, leading to seizures. Seizures occur when there is a sudden surge of abnormal electrical impulses in the brain. The presence of a tumor can disturb the normal functioning of brain cells and their communication, leading to these abnormal electrical discharges and subsequent seizures. 3. Cognitive and Behavioral Changes: Depending on the tumor's location, cognitive and behavioral changes may occur. Tumors in areas responsible for cognitive function, such as the frontal or temporal lobes, can affect memory, concentration, language skills, and problem-solving abilities. Tumors can also cause personality changes, mood swings, irritability, or depression due to the disruption of normal brain function and chemical imbalances caused by the tumor. It is important to note that these symptoms are not exclusive to brain tumors and can be caused by other conditions as well. If Sam experiences any of these symptoms, it is crucial for him to seek medical attention to undergo proper evaluation and receive an accurate diagnosis.

The launch of the 100 Mile Swim is expected to generate significant interest from the global media and supporters. Agius's previous successful world record attempts have been covered by major news outlets around the world, and the 100 Mile Swim is likely to attract even more attention.
